title: Correlation is not causation: confounders and reverse causality

videos.script: Horta's marketing team noticed something odd. Deliveries that used a free-delivery coupon took almost ten minutes longer than deliveries that did not. The difference was statistically significant. Does a coupon slow a courier down? {{coupon}} Of course not. Coupons were sent mostly to Barão Geraldo, the far neighbourhood, and far deliveries take longer whether they carry a coupon or not. Distance caused both. {{distance}} That is the most common way a correlation misleads: a third thing, a confounder, drives both of the things you measured. {{confounder}} There are others. The arrow can point the other way from the one you assumed. The pattern can be chance, especially in data that drifts over time. And the way the data was collected can create a pattern that is not there in the world. {{others}} One of these tricks can even reverse a result. Horta's motorbikes are on time more often than its bicycles on short trips, and on long trips too, and still less often overall. {{reverse}} This lesson takes each trap in turn, and ends with the one method that removes all of them at once: letting a coin decide. {{coin}}
